keyVerseText: Which came with Zerubbabel: Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel: Seraiah: also called, Azariah, nehe.7.7.
rootMeaning: The name בִּלְשָׁן (Bilshân) is of uncertain derivation, with no clear root word provided. However, the lexicon suggests a possible connection to the idea of inquiry or investigation, as seen in related Late Hebrew and Aramaic terms. This nuance of being an 'inquirer' or one who seeks information adds depth beyond a simple proper name, indicating a person characterized by attentiveness or discernment rather than just a label.
usageInScripture: Bilshan appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a proper name referring to an Israelite who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The consistent translation simply preserves the name without additional interpretation, highlighting its role as an individual within the post-exilic community. This limited but focused usage emphasizes Bilshan's identity as part of the faithful remnant restoring Israel after captivity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Bilshan as an individual who returned with Zerubbabel underscores the faithfulness of God's people in the fulfillment of His promises to restore Israel. The possible meaning of 'inquirer' resonates with the believer's call to seek God diligently and to be attentive to His word during times of renewal. This name reminds us that God preserves and uses faithful individuals to accomplish His redemptive purposes, pointing forward to the ultimate restoration found in Christ. Recognizing Bilshan's place in the post-exilic community encourages believers to embrace their role in God's ongoing work of restoration and covenant faithfulness.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 2:2 lists Bilshan among the leaders who returned with Zerubbabel, emphasizing his inclusion in the collective effort to rebuild Israel. The verse connects Bilshan with other notable figures, highlighting the unity and purpose of this group. The mention of Bilshan here not only identifies him as part of this historic return but also symbolizes the faithful remnant responding to God's call to restoration, reinforcing the theme of divine faithfulness and communal renewal.
